Outliers and dataset tests

Source: vignettes/outliers.Rmd
outliers.Rmd

Six tests compare a record with the other records of its species or its dataset instead of with reference data: outlier (geographic outliers within a species), the three fossil outlier tests, and the two dataset tests dataset_ddmm and dataset_rounded, which look for conversion and gridding errors in a dataset’s coordinates as a whole. They are CoordinateCleaner’s cc_outl(), cf_age(), cf_outl(), cf_range(), cd_ddmm() and cd_round(). Because a group has to be complete before any of its records can be judged, these tests run in a pass of their own over the whole input before the record tests. This article runs the geographic and dataset tests on a simulated table of alpine plants, adds the artificial-hotspot test aohi, and shows how the group pass works on streamed input. The fossil outlier tests are shown in the fossil article. Installation is covered in Get started.

library(OccurrenceCleaner)

Example data 

set.seed(11)
sp <- data.frame(species = c("Erica carnea", "Gentiana verna", "Pinus mugo", "Salix retusa"),
                 lon = c(12, 10, 14, 11), lat = c(47, 46.5, 47.5, 46.8), sd = c(1.5, 2, 1, 1.2),
                 n = c(400, 250, 300, 6))
x <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(sp)), function(i)
  data.frame(species = sp$species[i], decimalLongitude = round(rnorm(sp$n[i], sp$lon[i], sp$sd[i]), 5),
             decimalLatitude = round(rnorm(sp$n[i], sp$lat[i], sp$sd[i] / 2), 5))))
x$datasetKey <- sample(c("survey-a", "survey-b", "herbarium"), nrow(x), TRUE)
x$truth <- "clean"

The table has 961 records of four alpine plants around the Eastern Alps, spread over three datasets; Salix retusa has only 6 records. Into it go four herbarium records placed on the wrong continent or far outside the species’ area (New York, Sydney, Paris, Moscow), one more Pinus mugo record inside its area as a control, and two datasets of 300 records each with the errors the dataset tests look for: an atlas whose coordinates were converted from degrees and minutes as if they were decimals, so that no decimal part exceeds .59, and an atlas published on the centres of a quarter-degree grid:

far <- data.frame(species = c("Erica carnea", "Erica carnea", "Gentiana verna", "Pinus mugo", "Pinus mugo"),
                  decimalLongitude = c(-74.0, 151.2, 2.35, 12.1, 37.6), decimalLatitude = c(40.7, -33.9, 48.86, 47.3, 55.8),
                  datasetKey = "herbarium", truth = c("far", "far", "far", "clean", "far"))
ddmm <- data.frame(species = sample(sp$species[1:3], 300, TRUE),
                   decimalLongitude = floor(runif(300, 8, 16)) + sample(0:59, 300, TRUE) / 100,
                   decimalLatitude = floor(runif(300, 45, 48)) + sample(0:59, 300, TRUE) / 100,
                   datasetKey = "atlas-ddmm", truth = "ddmm")
grid <- data.frame(species = sample(sp$species[1:3], 300, TRUE),
                   decimalLongitude = round(runif(300, 8, 16) * 4) / 4 + 0.125,
                   decimalLatitude = round(runif(300, 45, 48) * 4) / 4 + 0.125,
                   datasetKey = "atlas-grid", truth = "grid")
x <- rbind(x, far, ddmm, grid)
table(x$datasetKey, x$truth)
#>             
#>              clean ddmm far grid
#>   atlas-ddmm     0  300   0    0
#>   atlas-grid     0    0   0  300
#>   herbarium    302    0   4    0
#>   survey-a     326    0   0    0
#>   survey-b     329    0   0    0

Geographic outliers 

f <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = c("invalid", "outlier"))
table(truth = f$truth, outlier = f$flag_outlier)
#>        outlier
#> truth   FALSE TRUE
#>   clean   957    0
#>   ddmm    300    0
#>   far       1    3
#>   grid    300    0

Three of the four far records are flagged and no clean record is. For each species the test takes every record’s mean distance to the species’ other records and flags those above Q75 + 5 x IQR of these means, CoordinateCleaner’s default. The Gentiana verna record in Paris stays below that fence: the simulated Gentiana records spread over about 2 degrees of longitude around 10 E, so a point 7.6 degrees west raises the mean distance less than the fence allows. Salix retusa, with 6 distinct points, is below min_occs = 7 and is not tested.

The fence and the statistic are set through settings. With method = "mad" the fence is median + 5 x MAD, with method = "distance" a record is flagged when its nearest other record of the species is more than tdi km away (1000 km by default):

m <- sapply(c("quantile", "mad", "distance"), function(meth)
  tapply(flag_occurrences(x, tests = "outlier", settings = list(outlier = list(method = meth)))$flag_outlier,
         x$truth, sum))
knitr::kable(m)
quantile mad distance
clean 0 3 0
ddmm 0 9 0
far 3 4 3
grid 0 3 0

The MAD fence is the stricter one here: it catches all four far records but also 15 records inside the species’ areas, most of them in the converted atlas, whose coordinates are shifted towards the south-west of each degree square. The distance method flags the same three far records as the quantile fence; the Paris record is within 1000 km of Gentiana records in the Alps. The map shows the default result:

plot(f, type = "map", rules = list(outlier = "outlier"))

CoordinateCleaner’s sampling correction leaves outliers unflagged in countries with few records, where an isolated record is more likely a real but poorly documented population than an error. It needs the number of records per country; with that table, sampling_thresh keeps an outlier flagged only in countries whose record density lies above that quantile of all countries’ densities:

counts <- data.frame(country = c("US", "AU", "FR", "RU", "AT", "DE", "IT", "CH", "SI"),
                     records = c(4e8, 1.2e8, 1e8, 6e6, 2.5e7, 1.8e8, 5e7, 4e7, 6e6))
fs <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = c("invalid", "outlier"), gazetteers = list(sampling = counts),
                       settings = list(outlier = list(sampling_thresh = 0.25)))
x[fs$flag_outlier != f$flag_outlier, c("species", "decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude")]
#>          species decimalLongitude decimalLatitude
#> 957 Erica carnea            -74.0            40.7
#> 958 Erica carnea            151.2           -33.9
#> 961   Pinus mugo             37.6            55.8

Russia, Australia and the United States have the three lowest densities in this table, at or below its 25 % quantile, so the outlier flags on the records in Moscow, Sydney and New York are lifted. The counts here are illustrative. Real ones come from rgbif::occ_count(country = ...) for each country, or from a tally of the input itself; the table is recorded in the reference label by size and checksum.

Species with many records

For a species with 10,000 records or more the pairwise distances are replaced by a raster approximation, as in CoordinateCleaner: records are counted on a 0.5-degree grid spanning the whole input, the statistic is computed between grid cells with distances weighted by the cell counts, and the records of the outlier cells are flagged. settings = list(outlier = list(thinning = TRUE)) uses the grid for every species, and thinning_res sets the cell size. A species of 15,001 records with one record in Madrid:

big <- data.frame(species = "Rhododendron ferrugineum",
                  decimalLongitude = c(rnorm(15000, 11, 1.5), -3.7),
                  decimalLatitude = c(rnorm(15000, 46.8, 0.6), 40.4))
system.time(fb <- flag_occurrences(big, tests = "outlier"))
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>    0.03    0.00    0.03
which(fb$flag_outlier)
#> [1] 15001

The Madrid record is the only one flagged. CoordinateCleaner 3.0.1 computes the same cell statistics but never flags a record on this path, because its mapping from the outlier cells back to records returns none; the article Coming from CoordinateCleaner shows the comparison.

Dataset tests 

d <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = c("invalid", "dataset_ddmm", "dataset_rounded"))
knitr::kable(aggregate(as.data.frame(d)[c("flag_dataset_ddmm", "flag_dataset_rounded")],
                       by = list(dataset = d$datasetKey), FUN = all))
dataset flag_dataset_ddmm flag_dataset_rounded
atlas-ddmm TRUE FALSE
atlas-grid FALSE TRUE
herbarium FALSE FALSE
survey-a FALSE FALSE
survey-b FALSE FALSE

dataset_ddmm flags every record of the converted atlas and dataset_rounded every record of the gridded one; the three datasets of clean records pass both. The dataset key is datasetKey, GBIF’s identifier of the publishing dataset, and can be set with occ_columns(dataset = ...). Records without a key are not tested. The two tests read different signs, which the decimal parts of the coordinates show:

library(ggplot2)
dec <- data.frame(dataset = x$datasetKey,
                  lon = x$decimalLongitude %% 1, lat = x$decimalLatitude %% 1)
dec <- dec[dec$dataset %in% c("survey-a", "atlas-ddmm", "atlas-grid"), ]
ggplot(dec, aes(lon, lat)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8, colour = "#2E6F9E") +
  facet_wrap(~dataset) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1)) +
  labs(x = "decimal part of longitude", y = "decimal part of latitude") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 17) +
  theme(panel.spacing = unit(2, "lines"),
        panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
        plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA))

In a dataset of correct decimal coordinates the decimal parts fill the unit square. After a degree-minute conversion they stay below .6 on both axes, so the square’s upper and right bands are empty; dataset_ddmm tests that with a binomial test on a 1000 x 1000 grid of decimal values. On a grid the decimals take a few values only, and dataset_rounded finds the regular spacing in the autocorrelation of the coordinate histograms of each axis. The degree-minute atlas is not on a grid and the gridded atlas has decimal parts of .125, .375, .625 and .875 on both axes, so each fails one test only.

Artificial hotspots 

ah <- reference_points("aohi")
h <- data.frame(species = "Erica carnea", decimalLongitude = ah$lon[ah$taxon == "Plantae"][1:3] + 0.03,
                decimalLatitude = ah$lat[ah$taxon == "Plantae"][1:3])
data.frame(hotspot = ah$notes[ah$taxon == "Plantae"][1:3],
           flagged = flag_occurrences(h, tests = "aohi")$flag_aohi)
#>                       hotspot flagged
#> 1            zero coordinates    TRUE
#> 2  Reserva Natural La Planada    TRUE
#> 3 center of a 4km grid square    TRUE

aohi flags records within 10 km of a point of the Artificial Hotspot Occurrence Inventory (Park et al. 2023): the coordinates that recur most often in GBIF plant, bird, insect and mammal records, such as (0, 0), a nature reserve or the centre of a mapping-grid square. The inventory’s notes and determination columns say why a point recurs and whether it is a real observation site, so it can be filtered before use (see the article on custom gazetteers).

One rule over all of them 

all_f <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = c("invalid", "outlier", "dataset_ddmm", "dataset_rounded", "aohi"))
t <- tally_flags(all_f, by = "datasetKey",
                 rules = list(grouped = c("outlier", "dataset_ddmm", "dataset_rounded", "aohi")))
knitr::kable(t[, c("datasetKey", "n", "flagged_outlier", "flagged_dataset_ddmm",
                   "flagged_dataset_rounded", "flagged_aohi", "removed_grouped", "kept_grouped")])
datasetKey n flagged_outlier flagged_dataset_ddmm flagged_dataset_rounded flagged_aohi removed_grouped kept_grouped
atlas-ddmm 300 0 300 0 1 300 0
atlas-grid 300 0 0 300 3 300 0
herbarium 306 3 0 0 4 6 300
survey-a 326 0 0 0 0 0 326
survey-b 329 0 0 0 0 0 329

The two atlases are removed whole. The herbarium loses 6 records: the 3 outliers and 4 records near inventory points, one of them both. The New York record lies 5 km from Central Park, a bird hotspot. The Paris record that the outlier test kept lies 3.7 km from the centre of a 10 km grid square used for French plant records, and two clean records in Bavaria lie near centres of the German floristic mapping grid. The aohi flags in the atlases are of the same kind, so whether to keep them depends on whether a record at a grid centre is acceptable for the analysis.

Streamed input

On an on-disk table the group pass reads every input file before the record pass: once to count records per species and to collect the coordinate ranges of each dataset, and once more to collect the records of each group. Small species and fossil taxa go through hashed bucket files in the output directory, large species are counted on the grid, and datasets are summarised as they stream, so memory does not grow with the input. A species or dataset spread over several files is tested as one group. The result is kept in group_result.rds in the output directory, so a resumed run does not repeat the group pass. The same table split into three files gives the same tally as the data frame:

src <- file.path(tempdir(), "parts"); dir.create(src, showWarnings = FALSE)
for (i in 1:3) vectra::write_vtr(x[seq(i, nrow(x), 3), ], file.path(src, sprintf("part-%d.vtr", i)))
out <- file.path(tempdir(), "flags-grouped")
s <- flag_occurrences(src, tests = c("invalid", "outlier", "dataset_ddmm", "dataset_rounded"),
                      out = out, keep = c("species", "datasetKey"), verbose = FALSE)
st <- tally_flags(s, by = "datasetKey", rules = list(grouped = c("outlier", "dataset_ddmm", "dataset_rounded")))
identical(st$removed_grouped, tally_flags(flag_occurrences(x, tests = c("invalid", "outlier", "dataset_ddmm",
                                                                       "dataset_rounded")),
                                          by = "datasetKey",
                                          rules = list(grouped = c("outlier", "dataset_ddmm", "dataset_rounded")))$removed_grouped)
#> [1] TRUE

The flags agree record by record as well; the package’s tests check that for every grouped test, including the fossil tests with their random age draws.

Practical guidance

  • A grouped flag depends on the rest of the input. Adding records of a species can turn an outlier into a normal record, and removing a dataset’s records changes nothing for the other datasets. Run the grouped tests on the table that goes into the analysis, after taxonomic filtering, not on a larger extract.

  • The quantile fence is the conservative default. At Q75 + 5 x IQR it flagged three of four far records and no clean one here; the MAD fence flagged all four plus 15 records inside the species’ areas. mltpl moves either fence.

  • Species below min_occs distinct points are not tested. With fewer than 7 points the spread of the distances says little; min_occs can be raised, not usefully lowered below a handful.

  • The dataset tests need a dataset key and a reasonable span. dataset_ddmm tests only datasets spanning at least min_span degrees (2) on both axes; dataset_rounded needs at least min_unique_ds_size distinct points (4) and reads histogram regularities, so a small or highly clustered dataset can be flagged by it without being gridded. Its result is best read per dataset, with tally_flags(by = "datasetKey"), before it goes into a rule.

  • A raster approximation answers a coarser question. For species of 10,000 records or more, a cell of 0.5 degrees is the unit: a single far record forms its own cell and is flagged, but an outlier cell next to the main range is not.

References

Park DS, Xie Y, Thammavong HT, Tulaiha R, Feng X (2023). Artificial Hotspot Occurrence Inventory (AHOI). Journal of Biogeography 50:441-449. doi:10.1111/jbi.14543

Zizka A, Silvestro D, Andermann T, Azevedo J, Duarte Ritter C, Edler D, Farooq H, Herdean A, Ariza M, Scharn R, Svanteson S, Wengström N, Zizka V, Antonelli A (2019). CoordinateCleaner: standardized cleaning of occurrence records from biological collection databases. Methods in Ecology and Evolution 10:744-751. doi:10.1111/2041-210X.13152
